before: ["firmly monergist", "Reformed-leaning", "balanced on grace", "Arminian-leaning", "firmly synergist"]
after: ["firmly monergist", "monergist-leaning", "balanced on grace", "synergist-leaning", "firmly synergist"]
why: Grace was the only axis whose bands named parties instead of poles, so confessional Lutherans (33), Thomist Catholics and dispensationalists were headlined 'Reformed-leaning', and the Orthodox coordinate, Molinist Catholics and Traditional Southern Baptists 'Arminian-leaning'. Seven blockers and eleven other findings converged on the pole-word pattern the other five axes already use.

before: Monergist / Synergist, used without definition anywhere on the page
after: Monergist / Synergist kept, each glossed once at first mention in the fair summary: 'Monergists (God alone brings a person to faith)' and 'Synergists (the person freely cooperates with the grace God gives)'
why: The rename proposals conflicted and each stranded a tradition ('Effectual grace' excludes Lutheran monergists who confess resistible grace; 'Sovereign grace' is one pole's boast). The verifiers' fallback, and the keep-verbatim list in mockery-36, was to keep the standard taxonomy and define the contested word where it first does work.

before: 'Monergists hold that salvation is God's work from beginning to end: he chooses, calls, and keeps his people, and his saving grace cannot finally be refused.'
after: Monergism is defined by the sinner contributing nothing to conversion, with the Reformed/Lutheran split on resistibility stated explicitly; a sentence added that most Baptist synergists hold believers are kept to the end; both poles glossed; a closing clause names both vocabularies ('Arminian or Wesleyan' and 'synergy')
why: Defining monergism by irresistible grace excluded confessional Lutherans from the pole the quiz itself codes them at, and putting perseverance only on the monergist side split the Baptist majority across the two paragraphs.

before: 5 entries: Augustine c. 411-430; Council of Orange 529; Luther 1525; Remonstrance/Dort 1610-19; Wesley/Whitefield 1740s
after: 9 entries: Augustine; Cassian c. 428; Second Council of Orange 529 (with its cooperation clause); Luther 1525; Trent 1547; Formula of Concord 1577; Dort 1610-19; Synod of Jerusalem 1672; Wesley/Whitefield 1739-41
why: The synergist pole had no pre-1610 advocate except Pelagius and Erasmus, so Catholics (55) and Orthodox (65) read that their view began with a Dutch protest; Lutherans, whom the quiz codes 'firmly monergist', had no landmark either; and the Wesley-Whitefield date was loose.

before: ["Romans 9", "Ephesians 1:3-11", "John 6:37-44", "1 Timothy 2:3-4", "2 Peter 3:9", "Hebrews 6:4-6"]
after: ["Romans 9", "Romans 8:28-30", "Ephesians 1:3-14", "John 6:37-44", "1 Timothy 2:3-4", "2 Peter 3:9", "Acts 7:51", "Philippians 2:12-13"]
why: Romans 8:28-30, the text both poles build on, was missing; the summary's synergist clauses had no verse (Acts 7:51 for resistance, Philippians 2:12-13 for cooperation); Ephesians 1:3-11 cut a Greek sentence mid-clause; Hebrews 6:4-6 is an apostasy text that cuts across the axis and implied the right pole means losing salvation.

before: left: Calvin, Sproul; right: Arminius (Works), Olson
after: left: Luther (The Bondage of the Will), Calvin, Sproul; right: John of Damascus (Exact Exposition II.29-30), Arminius (Declaration of Sentiments), Wesley (Predestination Calmly Considered), Olson
why: The monergist list equated the pole with Calvinism although the axis's own history names Luther's 1525 book; the synergist list described a pole held by Catholics (55) and Orthodox (65) with two Protestant Arminians only.

before: bands[2] = "centered on the sacraments"
after: bands[2] = "between sacramental and memorial"
why: The midpoint was labelled with the left pole's own noun and read as a doctrinal position stronger than 'sacramental-leaning', so a Baptist or Pentecostal at 50 was headlined with the word their confessions deliberately avoid.

before: '...baptism joins a person to Christ and his church, and so the children of believers are baptized... both are ordinances obeyed by believers rather than channels of grace.'
after: Poles defined by efficacy; infant baptism demoted to an indicator with both grounds named ('children of the covenant' or 'the washing of new birth'); the memorial half states the Supper as remembrance and proclamation and locates blessing in the faith of the receivers; a third sentence names the mixed positions (Reformed Baptist, Churches of Christ)
why: 'And so' derived paedobaptism from sacramental efficacy, which is neither the Reformed nor the Lutheran ground, and the memorial sentence denied Reformed Baptists a view their confession states (LBC 30.7).

before: 5 entries: Ignatius c. 110; Lateran IV 1215 ('defines transubstantiation'); Zurich 1525; Marburg 1529; Calvin 1559
after: 8 entries: Ignatius; John of Damascus c. 743; Lateran IV 1215 (with Trent 1551 named); Zwingli 1525-26; Zurich/Schleitheim 1525-27; Marburg 1529 (stating what Luther and Zwingli each held); Calvin 1559; English Baptists 1609-89
why: The sacramental pole after Ignatius was represented only by a Western council the East does not receive; Lateran IV used the word but Trent defined it; Marburg never said what Luther held, the doctrine of the tradition coded at 15; and the memorial pole's largest family, the Baptists, had no entry and was filed under Anabaptism by omission.

before: ["John 6:53-58", "1 Corinthians 11:23-29", "Acts 2:38-39", "Colossians 2:11-12", "Romans 6:3-4", "Matthew 26:26-28"]
after: ["John 6:51-63", "Matthew 26:26-28", "1 Corinthians 11:23-29", "1 Corinthians 10:16-17", "Acts 2:38-41", "Colossians 2:11-12", "Romans 6:3-4", "Matthew 28:19-20", "Acts 8:36-38", "1 Peter 3:21"]
why: The page promises 'the passages each side reaches for', yet every baptism text was one paedobaptists cite and no credobaptist text appeared; 1 Corinthians 10:16-17, the text Article XXVIII, the Formula of Concord, Heidelberg 77 and Calvin all build on, was missing; and John 6 was cropped before v.63, the memorialist's verse from the same passage.

before: left: Schmemann, Mathison; right: Zwingli, Schreiner & Wright
after: left: Schmemann, Ratzinger, Bromiley (Children of Promise); right: Hubmaier, Schreiner & Crawford (The Lord's Supper), Schreiner & Wright
why: The pole where Catholics sit at 5 had no Catholic author and no infant-baptism title although two of three Table items are about baptism; the memorial pole was headed by the paedobaptist under whose Zurich the first Anabaptists were drowned. Zwingli moves to the history array, where his argument is now stated.

before: Sacramental / Memorial, with statement 5 asking about baptism's subjects
after: Poles unchanged; statement 5 replaced with a means-of-grace item so the axis measures efficacy, not credobaptism twice
why: Option (a) of the blocker: with the new statement 5 a 1689 Reformed Baptist scores 50 ('between sacramental and memorial') instead of 67 ('memorial-leaning'), and a Zwinglian Baptist still reaches 100. The pole rename to 'Ordinance' is recorded in disputed.

before: name: "Spirit"
after: name: "Gifts" (key 'spirit' unchanged, so tokens, CSS variables and statement axis ids are untouched)
why: The axis was named with the left pole's key word, so the share bar and headline read as if the cessationist had no Spirit.

before: ["continuationist", "open to the gifts", "undecided on the gifts", "cautious about the gifts", "cessationist"]
after: ["continuationist", "continuationist-leaning", "open but cautious on the gifts", "cessationist-leaning", "cessationist"]
why: 'Undecided on the gifts' called a settled, named position (Saucy's 'open but cautious' in Are Miraculous Gifts for Today?) indecision, and the old flanking bands split that position's name across two bands with an open/cautious valence asymmetry.

before: '...passed away once the apostolic foundation was laid and the New Testament was complete.' (ends there)
after: Continuationists are described as differing on how eagerly to seek the gifts; cessationists are given what they affirm (God still heals and answers prayer; the Spirit's ordinary work through Word and providence) and the canon argument is marked as an addition many make
why: The cessationist paragraph was purely negative, which is the caricature cessationists fight, and 'should be sought' described only the Pentecostal form of continuance while the Orthodox (35) and Catholics (40) are coded on that side.

before: 6 entries: Montanism 2nd c.; Chrysostom c. 390 ('the sign gifts had ceased'); Azusa 1906; Warfield 1918; charismatic renewal 1960s ('carries the gifts into Catholic churches'); Strange Fire 2013
after: 10 entries: Irenaeus + Montanism late 2nd c.; Chrysostom c. 390 (quoted); Augustine c. 426; Westminster/1689 1646; Wesley and the holiness movement 1749-1867; Topeka and Azusa 1901-06; Warfield 1918; charismatic renewal 1960s (Pentecostal-style practice entering, not the gifts arriving); third wave 1980s-90s; Four Views 1996 replacing the 2013 conference
why: The continuationist family tree was a condemned sect and a 1,500-year gap while the cessationist side had four entries; 'sign gifts' put a modern cessationist category in a fourth-century mouth; 'carries the gifts into Catholic churches' asserted an absence Catholic teaching denies; and cessationism looked like a reaction to Pentecostalism rather than a confessional position of 1646.

before: ["1 Corinthians 12-14", "1 Corinthians 13:8-12", "Acts 2:17-18", "Ephesians 2:20", "Hebrews 2:3-4", "Joel 2:28-29"]
after: ["1 Corinthians 14:1-5", "1 Corinthians 13:8-12", "Acts 2:17-18", "1 Thessalonians 5:19-21", "Ephesians 2:20", "Hebrews 2:3-4", "2 Corinthians 12:12"]
why: Joel 2:28-29 and Acts 2:17-18 are the same text and 1 Corinthians 13:8-12 sits inside 12-14, so the continuationist column was padded with duplicates against three cessationist texts; 1 Thessalonians 5:19-21 (the verse statement 9 paraphrases) and the cessationist flagship 2 Corinthians 12:12 were both missing. Now three per pole plus one read both ways.

before: left: Grudem, Storms; right: MacArthur (Strange Fire), Warfield
after: left: Grudem, Fee (Paul, the Spirit, and the People of God); right: Warfield, Gaffin (Perspectives on Pentecost)
why: The pole Pentecostals defined (coded 5) had no Pentecostal author, and the cessationist pole was represented by the book whose subtitle calls charismatic worship counterfeit; both cessationist-side reviewers asked for Gaffin instead.

before: left_pole: "Covenantal"
after: left_pole: "One people of God" (right pole 'Dispensational' unchanged, it being that side's own name)
why: 'Covenantal' is the name of Reformed federal theology, yet it was stamped on every non-dispensationalist: a strongly Orthodox or Catholic answer set produced the headline 'Sacramental, covenantal, rooted in tradition', and Lutherans, Anabaptists and Restorationists reject the system by name.

before: ["covenantal", "covenantal-leaning", "centered on the kingdom", "dispensational-leaning", "dispensational"]
after: ["one people of God", "leaning to one people of God", "balanced on Israel and the church", "dispensational-leaning", "dispensational"]
why: The midpoint named a position both poles claim (Vos and Ladd, McClain and Blaising & Bock all make the kingdom their centre), so a historic premillennialist at 50 was told he held a theology he does not, and the outer left bands carried the Reformed system's name onto Catholics, Orthodox, Lutherans and Mennonites.

before: '...Christ's kingdom is present now, with his return bringing the new creation.'
after: '...his return brings the new creation, for some after a millennial reign on earth', plus a closing sentence on progressive dispensationalism and Pentecostal use of the rapture without the system
why: The left pole was written as amillennialism only, so historic premillennialists who hold one people of God (Ladd, whom the axis's own history cites, and with him Spurgeon, Piper and Grudem) had no home on either side.

before: 6 entries: Augustine c. 413-426; Westminster 1646 (covenant of works and grace); Darby 1830s; Scofield 1909; Ladd 1950s; progressive dispensationalism 1990s ('softens the Israel-church distinction')
after: 10 entries: Justin and Irenaeus c. 155-180; Augustine; Augsburg XVII 1530; Westminster 1646 (reworded to the one-covenant claim); Darby 1830s (attributed to Darby, not the whole movement); Scofield 1909; Chafer and Ryrie 1924-65; Ladd 1950s; Nostra Aetate and the mainline statements 1965-96; progressive dispensationalism 1990s (stated in its own terms)
why: The right pole began in 1830 while the left began with Augustine, which reproduces the 'invented by Darby' polemic; the 1646 line described a Reformed system four of the five left-pole traditions do not hold; 'softens' was the critics' verb for a movement the page recommends; and the modern repudiation of replacement theology by Rome and the mainline was absent.

before: ["Romans 11", "Galatians 3:26-29", "Revelation 20:1-6", "Daniel 9:24-27", "1 Thessalonians 4:13-17", "Matthew 24", "Ephesians 2:11-22"]
after: ["Genesis 17:7-8", "Daniel 9:24-27", "Matthew 24", "Romans 11", "Galatians 3:26-29", "Ephesians 2:11-22", "1 Thessalonians 4:13-18", "Hebrews 8:6-13", "Revelation 20:1-6"] (canonical order, so the chips do not group by side)
why: The dispensational pole was represented only by timetable texts and had no Abrahamic covenant passage although statement 10 rests on one; the covenantal pole lacked the new-covenant text its own read-more authors argue from.

before: left: Horton (Introducing Covenant Theology), Riddlebarger
after: left: Riddlebarger, Ladd (The Gospel of the Kingdom)
why: Under the heading for a pole held by Catholics, Orthodox, Lutherans, Methodists, Anabaptists and Baptists, the first title argued infant baptism from the covenant of grace; Ladd is already named in the axis history, is a Baptist and a premillennialist, and is accepted by the other pole as its classic interlocutor.

before: name: "Tradition"
after: name: "Authority" (key 'tradition' unchanged)
why: The axis was named after one pole's key word while its own midpoint band already said 'balanced on authority'.

before: left_pole: "With tradition"
after: left_pole: "Scripture and tradition" (right pole 'Scripture alone' unchanged)
why: 'With tradition' was not parallel to 'Scripture alone', broke every sentence the code builds from a pole name ('70% toward With tradition'), and removed the word Scripture from the pole whose holders say they hold Scripture and Tradition together (Trent Sess. IV; Dei Verbum 9).

before: bands[3] = "Scripture-first"
after: bands[3] = "Scripture over tradition"
why: 'Scripture-first' implies the other pole puts Scripture second, which Dei Verbum 21 and Orthodox usage deny, and no Protestant tradition uses the phrase of itself; 'Scripture over tradition' is a description both sides recognise as the real point of difference.

before: '...the creeds, councils, and the church's teaching office...' / '...agree that tradition can be a valuable guide...'
after: Left pole: creeds, ecumenical councils, the consensus of the Fathers and the church's living teaching, with the teaching office marked as the Catholic form. Right pole: creeds and confessions may carry real but subordinate authority, only Scripture is infallible, any council may err, nothing may be required as an article of faith that Scripture does not prove
why: 'Teaching office' is Roman magisterium vocabulary and the Orthodox, coded at 5, have none; and 'tradition can be a valuable guide' described biblicism rather than the confessional sola scriptura the pole's own recommended book (Mathison) exists to distinguish.

before: 5 entries, 4 of them for the tradition pole: Vincent 434; Trent 1546; Westminster 1646; Newman 1845; Dei Verbum 1965
after: 8 entries: Basil c. 375; Vincent 434; Second Nicaea 787; Worms 1521; Trent 1546; Formula of Concord 1577; Westminster 1646; Dei Verbum 1965 (the Newman line removed, as historian-1 offers, since Newman remains the first read-more title)
why: On the axis whose right pole is 'Scripture alone' the Reformation's founding moment was missing entirely and the tradition pole was three-quarters Roman with no Eastern source, though Orthodoxy is coded furthest left.

before: 6 texts, no council passage and no Galatians 1
after: ["2 Thessalonians 2:15", "2 Timothy 3:16-17", "1 Timothy 3:15", "Acts 17:11", "Acts 15:6-29", "Matthew 15:3-9", "John 16:13", "Galatians 1:8-9"], alternating by pole
why: Statement 13 is about councils yet the one council in Scripture was absent, and the Scripture-alone pole lacked its sharpest text.

before: right: Mathison, Barrett
after: right: Mathison, T. Campbell (Declaration and Address)
why: A reader who scores 100 on this axis was handed only books arguing against the position that produces a 100; the Restoration primary source states the far end of the pole in its holders' own words.

before: ["liturgical", "liturgy-leaning", "flexible in worship", "informal in worship", "free in worship"]
after: ["liturgical", "liturgy-leaning", "between liturgical and free", "free-leaning in worship", "free in worship"]
why: Regulative-principle Presbyterians and Reformed Baptists land mid-axis and were told they are 'flexible in worship', the one adjective their rule of worship excludes; and 'informal' judged manner rather than form, so ordered Baptist, Old Order Anabaptist and produced charismatic services were all called informal.

before: 'Liturgical worship follows a set order, the church calendar, and a weekly Eucharist... Free worship keeps the form open so that the Spirit can lead in the moment, with an emphasis on spontaneity, sincerity, and the participation of the whole congregation.'
after: Liturgical: set order and calendar, 'usually' with the Eucharist at the centre, the whole congregation praying with the historic church and joining the worship of heaven. Free: Scripture prescribes no fixed liturgy, so each congregation orders its own service, some keeping a plain settled pattern and others leaving the shape open for the Spirit, with room for any member to contribute
why: Weekly Eucharist as a definition excluded three centuries of Prayer Book practice; 'sincerity' and 'the participation of the whole congregation' were claimed for one pole although 'full, conscious and active participation' is the liturgical movement's own watchword; and defining the free pole by spontaneity left the planned non-liturgical majority (Baptist, Bible church, Reformed, Anabaptist) with no home.

before: 6 entries: Didache; Justin c. 155; Cranmer 1549; Puritans 1600s; Finney 1830s; Jesus movement 1970s-
after: 10 entries: Didache; Justin c. 155 (with 'according to his ability'); the Eastern and Western eucharistic prayers 4th-6th c.; Zwingli and Luther 1525-26; Cranmer 1549 (full sentence); Puritans, Hooker and the Westminster Directory 1572-1645; Finney 1830s; Azusa Street 1906; Sacrosanctum Concilium 1963; contemporary worship 1970s-
why: The liturgical side's first named liturgy was Anglican and its history stopped in 1549, while the free side ran to Hillsong; the regulative principle was dated a century late; and the axis Pentecostals define had no Pentecostal entry.

before: ["Acts 2:42", "John 4:23-24", "1 Corinthians 14:26-40", "Colossians 3:16", "Hebrews 12:28", "Psalm 150"]
after: adds "Acts 20:7" and "Revelation 4-5"
why: The item on weekly communion had no supporting text, and the liturgical pole's central warrant, the heavenly liturgy, was absent.

before: left: Schmemann, Webber; right: Frame (Worship in Spirit and Truth), Kauflin
after: left: Schmemann, Ratzinger (The Spirit of the Liturgy); right: Hayford (Worship His Majesty), Kauflin
why: Frame's book is a Reformed defence of the regulative principle filed under a pole defined by the Spirit leading in the moment, and the largest free-worship family had no author on its own pole; the liturgical list had no Catholic title although Catholics are coded at 10.

before: Before anyone does anything, God has already chosen who will be saved, and his choice cannot fail.
after: God's choice of who will be saved is not based on anything he foresaw they would do.
why: Double-barreled, and both barrels are affirmed by synergists: Arminius, Wesley, the Orthodox (Dositheus, Decree 3) and the Southern Baptist Traditional Statement all hold an eternal, certain election grounded in foreknowledge, so the item did not discriminate monergism at all.

before: A person can genuinely resist God's grace and refuse salvation to the very end.
after: A person whom God is drawing to salvation can still finally refuse him and be lost.
why: As written a five-point Calvinist can honestly agree (WCF 10.4 and Dort III/IV: the non-elect resist the outward call to the end), so the item failed to separate the poles, and 'to the very end' read to Baptists as the perseverance question they answer the other way.

before: Saving faith is itself a gift God gives to those he has chosen, not the reason he chose them.
after: God alone works saving faith in a person; the sinner contributes nothing to conversion, not even the decision to believe.
why: The first clause is affirmed by Trent (Sess. VI ch. 8), Arminius, Wesley and Chrysostom alike, so only the subordinate clause discriminated and respondents had to guess which was keyed; with statement 1 now carrying election, statement 3 carries the monergism of conversion.

before: In the Lord's Supper, Christ is truly present in a way that goes beyond a symbol.
after: In the Lord's Supper, Christ himself is given through the bread and wine, not only remembered.
why: 'Truly present' was read by Mennonites, charismatics and Pentecostals of Christ present in the gathered congregation, so they were scored sacramental without holding a means-of-grace view; naming the elements locates the claim where the poles actually divide.

before: Baptism is an outward sign of a decision to follow Christ that has already been made.
after: Baptism is a public testimony to a faith already held, not a means by which God gives grace.
why: 'Outward sign' is the paedobaptist catechism definition of a sacrament and 'decision' is revivalist vocabulary that confessional credobaptists reject, so the item measured baptismal candidacy twice (with statement 6) and never asked the efficacy question the axis is named for.

before: The infants of believing parents should be baptized.
after: Infants should be baptized, not only those who profess faith for themselves.
why: 'The infants of believing parents' is verbatim Westminster covenant-household idiom (WCF 28.4); Rome, the East, Lutherans and the Prayer Book ground infant baptism differently.

before: Tongues, prophecy, and healing continue in the church today, as they did in Acts.
after: The gifts of tongues, prophecy, and healing are still given to the church today.
why: 'As they did in Acts' added a restorationist claim about manner and scale that Anglicans, Catholics, Orthodox, Methodists and Reformed continuationists do not make, so non-cessationists were pushed toward the cessationist pole; naming them as gifts stops cessationists who pray for the sick from agreeing by accident.

before: The miraculous sign gifts ended with the apostles or the completion of the New Testament.
after: The miraculous gifts of tongues, prophecy, and healing ended with the apostles or the completion of the New Testament.
why: 'Sign gifts' is a category used only inside cessationist writing and rejected by the continuationists the page recommends, so the quiz's own voice asked one side to answer inside the other's frame; both grounds of cessation are kept.

before: A modern-day prophecy should be weighed carefully, but it can genuinely come from the Spirit.
after: The Spirit still gives some Christians specific prophetic words for the church today.
why: The item led with a concession every cessationist grants (test everything) and left 'prophecy' undefined, so a cessationist who allows Spirit-given impressions could agree and be scored continuationist.

before: God's promises to national Israel will be fulfilled literally in a future earthly kingdom.
after: God will yet give national Israel its promised land and kingdom on this earth.
why: 'Fulfilled literally' is Ryrie's sine qua non used as the neutral frame, so covenantal readers were told in the item that they do not read Scripture literally.

before: The church is the true Israel, heir to every promise God made to Abraham.
after: There is one people of God across both testaments: the church, Jew and Gentile together, inherits the promises to Abraham.
why: The axis's only left-keyed item was written as hard supersessionism, which Rome (Nostra Aetate 4), the Orthodox, the Church of England, PCUSA, ELCA and UMC have all formally disowned, so the least dispensational Christians in the world were pushed a third of an axis to the right for refusing a description they are on record against; the new wording is the fair summary's own and is what dispensationalism denies by definition.

before: Believers will be caught up to meet Christ before a seven-year tribulation.
after: The church is a new body begun at Pentecost, not the continuation of Old Testament Israel.
why: A third of the axis was spent on rapture timing, which Ryrie's own sine qua non exclude, so post-tribulational and pre-wrath dispensationalists were scored 67 and matched to 'Southern Baptist'; the replacement is the movement's actual distinctive.

before: The creeds and councils of the early church carry real authority, not just historical interest.
after: The early creeds and councils carry an authority of their own, not only as faithful summaries of what Scripture teaches.
why: 'Real authority' did not distinguish ministerial from magisterial authority, so every confessional Protestant agreed and was pushed toward the tradition pole; the new wording is denied by Article XXI, WCF 31, LBC 1.10 and the Formula's Rule and Norm, and affirmed by Rome and the East.

before: Every doctrine must be proven from Scripture alone; tradition can never bind the conscience.
after: Only Scripture is infallible; every creed, council, and teacher can err and must be tested by it.
why: Two claims the Anglican and Lutheran formularies answer differently (Article VI yes, Article XXXIV and FC X no), so the magisterial Reformation position collapsed to Unsure; infallibility is the line the poles actually divide on.

before: The church, not the individual reader, is the final interpreter of Scripture.
after: When Christians disagree about a passage, the church's teaching office (bishops, councils, or a magisterium) has the final say.
why: A false dichotomy in one side's apologetic vocabulary: magisterial Protestants deny both limbs (WCF 1.9-10), so they could not answer honestly, and Anabaptists and congregational Baptists read 'the church' as the gathered congregation and were scored toward Rome.

before: Worship should follow a set liturgy that connects us to the historic church.
after: Worship should follow a fixed written liturgy, with set prayers used week by week.
why: The rationale clause made disagreement read as disowning connection to the historic church, which Puritan, Reformed Baptist and Anabaptist congregations claim as strongly as anyone, and 'set liturgy' was ambiguous between a fixed order and a prayer book.

before: Worship should be free-form and led by the Spirit in the moment.
after: Each congregation should shape its own order of service rather than follow a prescribed liturgy.
why: The item measured spontaneity rather than non-liturgical worship and made disagreement feel like denying the Spirit, so the largest free-church families (Baptist, Bible church, Mennonite, Churches of Christ) had no honest answer and were pulled toward the liturgical pole, while liturgical charismatics were misplaced the other way.

before: Communion should be celebrated every week as the center of the service.
after: The church year, with Advent, Lent, and Easter, should shape what a congregation reads, sings, and prays.
why: Weekly communion is not a liturgical marker: it pushed Churches of Christ and the Plymouth Brethren, the freest congregations that exist, toward 'liturgical', and pushed Prayer Book Anglicans, whose rubric requires communion three times a year, toward 'free'. The church year tests set form and cross-loads on nothing.

before: 18 statements, keying 2:1 per axis, five axes left-keyed
after: 18 statements kept (the demo and apply.js assume 6 axes and 18 statements); 17 balanced, opposite-keyed candidates added in a new candidate_statements array for the v1 four-to-six item build, including the perseverance item wesleyan-20 asks for
why: Acquiescence still produces a coherent profile (all-agree gives 33/33/33/67/33/33), which cannot be fixed inside three items per axis; the candidates make the v1 expansion a rewrite of the item pool rather than a redesign. lutheran-6 asks for the manducatio item that separates Lutheran from Reformed sacramental teaching; it is in the candidates, since the Table coordinates were compressed instead for the demo.

after: "Catholic (Roman and Eastern)" [72, 5, 22, 15, 5, 5]
why: Spirit 40 made the church that requires verified miracles for canonization look half cessationist, and tradition/worship at 10 against Orthodoxy's 5 penalised an answer set identical on 15 of 18 items, so a Catholic answering from the Catechism landed on Eastern Orthodox first. Grace rises because the revised statements 2 and 3 force Trent's cooperation language (Sess. VI ch. 5, can. 4). The rename covers the 23 Eastern Catholic churches.

Grace 65 put the Orthodox on the monergist side of the Wesleyans although synergeia is their own word for exactly this axis (Cassian, Dositheus Decree 3), and no Orthodox confession is cessationist while unction is a mystery and wonderworkers are canonized. The change also widens the Rome/Constantinople gap from 13 to 18 units.

Tradition 35 placed the tradition that wrote 'Scripture alone is the only rule and norm' left of centre on the authority axis; grace 20 and table 15 were unreachable by any honest confessional answer set; the revised statements 13-15 put a Book of Concord subscriber near 90.

Table 25 was 17-25 points from where Articles XXVII and XXVIII put a Prayer Book Anglican, so a typical Anglican landed on Roman Catholic first and Anglican second; Article XXI ('General Councils may err') puts the same respondent high on the revised authority axis.

before: "Presbyterian / Reformed" [10, 35, 75, 15, 45, 45]
after: "Presbyterian / Reformed (confessional)" [5, 10, 90, 5, 78, 40]
why: Table 35 was 18-35 points from where WCF 28-29 puts an adherent, so a PCA elder was handed 'Lutheran (confessional)' first at an identical 87%; the qualifier is added because the entry is a PCA/OPC/URC profile while the largest Presbyterian body in the US is mainline.

before: "Reformed Baptist" [10, 70, 80, 30, 55, 65]
why: Kingdom 30 made covenantal Baptists 'covenantal-leaning' though LBC ch. 7 and 31-32 have no rapture or tribulation; tradition 55 put the 1689 (whose 1.10 copies Westminster) at 'balanced on authority'; table 50 follows from the revised statement 5, which lets a confessional Baptist register the Supper as a means of grace; the qualifier separates the 1689 stream from the Reformed continuationists now given their own entry.

before: one entry, "Southern Baptist (typical)" [45, 85, 75, 70, 85, 70]
after: two entries: "Southern Baptist (non-Calvinist)" [80, 95, 75, 72, 95, 95] and "Southern Baptist (Calvinist)" [10, 95, 75, 72, 95, 95]
why: Grace 45 described no Southern Baptist: the convention is bimodal (about 30% of pastors Calvinist per LifeWay 2012, the rest signatories of the 2012 Traditional Statement), and the average made a historic-premillennial Traditionalist land on 'Anabaptist / Mennonite' first. '(typical)' also graded the adherent where the other qualifiers name a wing.

before: "Dispensational Bible church" [40, 90, 90, 95, 90, 75]
after: "Bible church (independent, dispensational)" [48, 95, 95, 95, 95, 95]
why: No congregation calls itself a 'Dispensational Bible church'; the self-name goes first and the system into a parenthetical, matching 'Lutheran (confessional)'. Worship rises because the revised statements 16-18 measure non-liturgical form rather than spontaneity.

Table 40 put the church of Articles XVII-XVIII and 'The Duty of Constant Communion' nearly halfway to memorialism, 32 points from where its own standards place a member; the entry also sat nearest the six-dimensional centre, so all-Unsure respondents were told they were Methodists.

before: "Pentecostal / Assemblies of God" [80, 85, 5, 75, 85, 90]
after: "Pentecostal (Assemblies of God, Church of God, COGIC)" [90, 90, 5, 75, 85, 95]
why: The name omitted the Church of God (Cleveland) and COGIC, the largest Pentecostal body in the United States, which share every coordinate.

Kingdom 60 put the Vineyard and Bethel stream on the dispensational side of a question their own theology (Ladd's inaugurated kingdom; Eberle & Trench) answers the other way; the moves also widen the Pentecostal/charismatic separation from 18.7 to 25.5 units without a seventh coordinate.

before: "Anabaptist / Mennonite" [75, 85, 55, 30, 70, 60]
after: "Anabaptist / Mennonite (peace church)" [90, 90, 30, 25, 90, 82]
why: Spirit 55 put Mennonites on the cessationist side of centre although no Anabaptist confession is cessationist; the qualifier warns a non-pacifist evangelical that the entry stands for a peace church, since no axis measures nonresistance, the ban or oaths.

target: tradition (added): Churches of Christ / Christian Churches
before: absent; a Stone-Campbell member's nearest traditions were 'Anabaptist / Mennonite, Wesleyan / Methodist' at 70% and 65%
why: About 2.5 million US adherents, and the middle of the Table axis (believer's immersion for the remission of sins with a weekly Supper) was empty; a simulated member now lands on the entry at 93%.

before: absent; a PCUSA member landed on 'Anglican (broad), Roman Catholic' with 'Presbyterian / Reformed' sixth
why: Roughly a tenth of US adults, and every Presbyterian, Lutheran and Methodist entry was coded at its confessional or evangelical wing.

before: absent; the monergist-continuationist quadrant was empty and the simulated member was 82.6 units from the nearest entry (66%)
why: The old coordinates encoded a grace-spirit correlation no confession asserts, while three of the page's own recommended authors (Grudem, Storms, Kauflin) come from this family; the member now lands at 95%.

before: absent; a Calvary Chapel profile was routed to 'Pentecostal / Assemblies of God', the tradition Chuck Smith defined the movement against
why: The dispensational, moderately continuationist, non-Pentecostal region was empty. The finding's second proposal, a separate Independent Baptist entry, is not applied: it would sit 20 units from the Bible church entry and recreate the twin-tradition problem.

target: tradition (added): National Baptist (NBC USA / historically Black Baptist)
before: absent; historically Black Baptists scattered between the Southern Baptist and Pentecostal entries
why: NBC USA is the second-largest Baptist body in the country. Grace is set from its New Hampshire Confession descent rather than from a style generalisation, and only the Gifts axis separates it from the Southern Baptist entry.

before: "take the three axes with the largest |score - 50|, join their band adjectives; if all six are within 10 of 50, label is 'A theological centrist'"
after: candidates restricted to axes outside the middle band, ties broken by the count of Strongly answers then by axis order, at most three; no candidates gives 'Near the center on every axis'
why: The old rule printed midpoint adjectives as convictions ('Firmly monergist, flexible in worship, centered on the sacraments' for someone who answered Unsure on four axes), and 'A theological centrist' presented the middle as a party. This is a code change; apply.js does not regenerate headline().

before: "match % = round(100 - distance / sqrt(6 * 100^2) * 100)" and an on-page note saying 'Match is 100 minus your distance across all six axes'
after: denominator 195 (the largest distance between two listed traditions), a tie rule at 10 units, a poor-fit hedge above 60 units, and suppression of the tradition line when all six axes are within 10 of 50
why: The 245-unit diagonal nobody spans inflated every match to 75-95%, an all-Unsure sheet returned 'Wesleyan / Methodist 83%', ties printed identical percentages in different ranks, and the published formula was not the one the code used. Code change.

before: scores stored as round(score/4) in base 32, so nine of thirteen reachable scores round-trip to a different value and 58 reopens as 60
after: documented base-13 encoding of round(score * 12 / 100), which round-trips every reachable score exactly
why: A shared link showed a different band from the one the sharer saw, on the one feature the launch test measures. Code change.

before: fill gauge ('Sacramental ○○○○○○○○○○ Memorial' for a fully sacramental respondent), 'Closest: X · Y', caption 'Filled circles run toward the pole named on the right'
after: position marker in eleven slots (one filled circle at round(score/10)), bar first so the columns align, 'Nearest on the map: X · Y' with the approximation caveat, caption 'The filled circle marks where you sit between the two poles named on each line'
why: The gauge read as a score of the virtue named, so every left-pole conviction posted as an empty bar under 'Grace', 'Spirit' or 'Tradition' - the single most screenshot-ready line in the product.

before: middle option labelled 'Unsure'
after: 'Unsure / neither', with one line above the first statement: 'If a statement is not the way your tradition frames the question, or you hold part of it and not the rest, choose Unsure / neither.'
why: The only midpoint recorded a considered 'neither' or 'not how we put it' as ignorance, which several traditions must answer on at least one item.

before: "Approximate positions of typical adherents, not official teaching. Match is 100 minus your distance across all six axes."
after: "Approximate positions of typical adherents, not official teaching. Match is 100% minus your distance from that tradition, as a share of the largest distance between any two traditions on this map. These six axes are the questions that split the Western churches at the Reformation: they do not measure church government, the papacy, or the peace-church convictions, so families that differ on those can sit close together here. Broad churches (Anglican, Methodist, mainline) are placed at their centre; their wings sit nearer other entries."
why: Rome and Constantinople are 18 units apart because nothing on the compass separates them; polity, the peace churches and the Anglican wings are likewise out of scope. Saying so is the honest alternative to a seventh axis the demo cannot carry.

before: "Demo build. Tradition positions are approximate; statements and histories should be reviewed before publishing."
after: "Demo build. Tradition positions are approximate sketches of typical adherents, not official teaching."
why: A builder's to-do told readers the content had not been checked, on a page whose promise is that it has been; after this audit it is also untrue.

before: lean() prints '58% toward Monergist' beside the band 'balanced on grace', and '50% · centered' at the midpoint
after: print the distance from centre as a percentage of the half-axis ('16% toward Monergist'), 'at the center' at 50, and 'at the Monergist pole' at 0/100
why: One net Agree out of six available points was rendered as a 58% majority lean, contradicting the band adjective printed next to it. Code change.
